newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, guerrillas wrap up sixth round of talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru, guerrillas wrap up sixth round of talks.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages in Lima wrapped up a sixth round of talks with the government on Tuesday, and a source close to doctors attending captives said the rebel leader's mood was darkening.

After negotiations lasting three hours in a Red Cross safehouse, the two sides agreed to continue their talks on Thursday. The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) negotiators were driven back to the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence across the street.

"The talks have continued in the same atmosphere as the previous meetings," Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, representing the Vatican as one of three guarantors for the negotiations, told reporters in a statement.
The talks will continue on Thursday, he said. The guarantors, who are sworn to secrecy, described earlier meetings as taking place "in a constructive atmosphere."

As negotiations to end the 70-day-old siege drag on, word of the state of the hostages and their captors came from a source close to medical teams which regularly enter the residence to provide check-ups.
The source told Reuters the hostages were in generally good spirits but MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa was increasingly morose.
"Cerpa looks irritated. He doesn't speak with everyone any more," said the source, who asked not to be named.

But the hostages, especially Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki and Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, were cheerful when the doctors entered the residence after the fourth round of talks with the government last Thursday.

"There is an atmosphere of optimism inside the residence. Some of them play chess, card games, ludo, and others read books so as not to be bored as they wait for whatever is going to happen," said the source.
"Cerpa's attitude has changed in the past few days. Before the meetings he was very talkative, but now he only speaks with ambassador Aoki and Tudela," the source said.
Hostages freed at the beginning of the crisis reported that the Tupac Amaru chief was courteous and approachable, even joining in round-table discussions on Peruvian politics.
While Cerpa now holds himself aloof from most of the hostages, his relationship with Aoki and Tudela has intensified since meeting with the government negotiators began on Feb. 11.
"Every time a meeting is over, they (Cerpa, Aoki and Tudela) get together and talk," the source said.

The hostages were mostly in good health. But two need to have medicines brought in from the outside for serious illnesses. Congressman Gilberto Siura suffers from stomach cancer, and former Supreme Court president Moises Pantoja has a heart condition and severe arthritis.
The doctors also examine the rebels if they request it.

"Once, two of the MRTA women asked the doctors, half joking but half seriously, if they could do a scan to see if they were pregnant," the source said, "Anyway, they did the tests and they were negative."

The 15-odd heavily-armed guerrillas siezed the residence during a coctail party to celebrate the Japanese emperor's birthday Dec. 17. Their chief demand is the freeing of 400 jailed comrades and their hostages include President Alberto Fujimori's brother, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two government ministers.
